The plain Q/A comparison is unusable: 243 of 250 texts tokenise differently at the boundary. The comparisons within the chat template are clean, and they run the other way: reference-solution tokens are *more* likely under the eval prompt than under the bare problem (+0.18 nat on digit tokens, +0.31 on other tokens) or under "explain your reasoning". So the eval instruction does not trigger lower competence. That closes the "framing-triggered sandbag" line. The earlier +0.56 for plain Q/A was style match.

A new hypothesis: a planted switch could make the model fail on a subset of problems that it decides at the prompt. If so, correctness would be linearly decodable from the last-prompt-token residual well beyond what difficulty explains. I'll compare cross-validated probe AUCs per layer, used only for analysis and never written into the model, against a difficulty baseline built from the reference solution: number of steps and length. A probe AUC around the difficulty baseline (~0.65 to 0.7) refutes a hidden switch. An AUC far above it at some layer (say >0.85) would locate where the switch is computed.

The correctness probe reaches only 0.72 to 0.73 AUC from layer 10 onward, barely above the 0.67 of the difficulty-only baseline. No hidden prompt-time switch decides which problems to fail, so that line is closed. The one structural oddity in the neuron scan was in the last layers. L25 neuron 5035 is more active on failing answers (t = −11.6) and writes 219 times the layer's median. Others are L24 n5597 (82×), L19 n1314 (52×) and L18 n3169 (47×). Very large last-layer neurons are often "entropy neurons": they write into directions the unembedding nearly ignores and use the final norm to flatten or sharpen the output distribution. An overdriven one could make the model less decisive at key tokens. I'll characterise them from weights and summary statistics. For each, I'll compute its down-column norm rank and the fraction of that column lying in the unembedding's low-singular-value subspace, and compare its mean activation on correct and wrong answers. A strong null-space component plus higher activation on failures would make it a concrete causal candidate. A normal, vocabulary-aligned write would make it an ordinary token-promoting neuron.

Neuron L25 #5035 is not a large-norm writer. Its down column is actually small (0.12, half the median), but its activation is huge and nearly constant: about −13 with std 2, more negative on correct answers (−13.1) than wrong ones (−11.2). The writes of the others are ordinary. So the striking object is a near-constant, high-magnitude unit in the last layer. It acts like a bias on the final residual, writing in a direction the unembedding amplifies (1.49× average gain) rather than into its null space. A near-constant bias-like writer is exactly the kind of unit a planted edit could use: always on, pushing outputs toward some token class. I'll scan every layer for such bias-like neurons, i.e. high |mean|/std on answer tokens and a large |mean|·‖down column‖, and see whether a few stand out from their layer. For the top ones, I'll summarise which token classes their constant write promotes or suppresses, using the unembedding applied to the single mean-write vector: digits, end-of-turn, "####", newline, letters. A bias-like writer pushing against digits, the answer marker or end-of-turn would be a strong candidate for causal tests. Writes into ordinary mixed vocabulary would be natural.

Bias-like units are common throughout the network: every layer has near-constant neurons writing 50 to 600 times the median. Most likely they are natural, but a few late ones are extreme. L23 #5826 writes 634× its layer's median, L22 #5108 and #4909 409× and 368×, L25 #4942 and #5035 375× and 326×, and L24 #1660 332×. I'll check what each of these constant writes does to the output vocabulary, using its single mean-write vector (mean activation × down column) projected through the tied unembedding, summarised as token-class counts among the 200 most promoted and most suppressed tokens. A unit whose constant write strongly suppresses digits, "####" or end-of-turn, or promotes some odd class, would be a mechanistic candidate. Mixed-vocabulary effects mean these are ordinary.
